extracted.intended_audience: readers and correspondents of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century public; essayists and contributors
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial aims and evaluative principles for composing and selecting Spectator papers and correspondence: what the paper will criticize or publish, its tone, scope (avoid private scandal and party quarrels), and some cultural commentaries (fashion, happiness, music, clubs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Address causes not mere surface dress
rubrics_metrics.description: 'it is not my Intention to sink the Dignity of this my Paper with Reflections upon Red-heels or Top-knots, but rather to enter into the Passions of Mankind, and to correct those depraved Sentiments that give Birth to all those little Extravagancies which appear in their outward Dress and Behaviour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confine criticism to particular fashions or ornaments; treat display of dress as symptom, and attack the underlying passions (vanity, taste, education) that produce such extravagancies. Example/anti-pattern: merely satirizing 'red-heels' or 'top-knots' without addressing the causes is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinguish vanity by treating root vices
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Foppish and fantastick Ornaments are only Indications of Vice, not criminal in themselves. Extinguish Vanity in the Mind, and you naturally retrench the little Superfluities of Garniture and Equipage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies should be aimed at 'first Seeds and Principles' rather than trivial externals; the editor considers moral correction preferable to mere mockery of fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish private scandal or intimate lampoons
rubrics_metrics.description: 'it is not my Design to be a Publisher of Intreagues and Cuckoldoms, or to bring little infamous Stories out of their present lurking Holes into broad Day light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper will not serve as a vehicle for private defamation or individual lampoons; correspondence full of private scandal, illegible lampoons, or personal calumnies will not be printed. If vice is attacked, it will be attacked as a class ('in a Body'), not by naming or making examples of particular persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid party partisanship; remain above faction
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I shall take Care to keep clear of every thing which looks that Way... I shall apply myself to it with my utmost Endeavours; but will never let my Heart reproach me with having done any thing towards encreasing those Feuds and Animosities that extinguish Religion, deface Government, and make a Nation miserable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spectator will not turn into a vehicle for party quarrels; it aims to allay private inflammations and public ferments, not inflame them. Writers/contributors should not press the paper into factional attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage innocent diversions and helpful submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'if he has any Materials that can furnish out an innocent Diversion, I shall promise him my best Assistance in the working of them up for a publick Entertainment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor invites correspondents to submit surprising stories, hints they cannot pursue, discoveries of epidemical vice, or accounts of uncommon virtue — provided these can furnish innocent/public-spirited entertainment. The editor will assist in shaping suitable contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed office: 'Censor of small Wares' to police fashion excesses
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I have Thoughts of creating an Officer under me to be entituled, _The Censor of small Wares_, and of allotting him one Day in a Week for the Execution of such his Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposed institutional remedy: appoint a regular correspondent/officer to note and correct recurring petty extravagances of dress and behaviour, acting like a surgeon (treating symptoms) while the editor treats the constitution (root causes). This formalizes frequency of attention to trivial fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating humor as social defense ('dare to be Ugly')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'it is, methinks, an honest and laudable Fortitude to dare to be Ugly... The best Expedient therefore is to be pleasant upon himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subject to ridicule for natural defects, the recommended tactic is cheerfulness and self-mockery; examples: Falstaff and Prince Harry use jest upon their own bodies to deflect mockery. Anti-pattern: excessive sensitivity or affectation about deformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of Deformity — explicit membership criteria for the 'Ugly Club'
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules (as given): I. 'That no Person whatsoever shall be admitted without a visible Quearity in his Aspect, or peculiar Cast of Countenance' (President decides). II. 'A singular Regard be had... to the Gibbosity of the Gentlemen... or to the Obliquity of their Figure.' III. 'That if the Quantity of any Man's Nose be eminently miscalculated, whether as to Length or Breadth, he shall have a just Pretence to be elected.' IV. 'That if there shall be two or more Competitors for the same Vacancy, caeteris paribus, he that has the thickest Skin to have the Preference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership is judged on visible deformity/peculiarities; governance by elected officers with casting vote for President. Ceremonial duties for new members: entertain the company with codfish and a speech in praise of Æsop; collect portraits of ill-favoured figures as club-room furniture. This is an explicit satirical rule-set for a convivial society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid half-and-half multilingual performance practice in opera
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The next Step to our Refinement, was the introducing of Italian Actors into our Opera; who sung their Parts in their own Language, at the same Time that our Countrymen perform'd theirs in our native Tongue... At length the Audience grew tir'd of understanding Half the Opera, and therefore to ease themselves Entirely of the Fatigue of Thinking, have so order'd it at Present that the whole opera is performed in an unknown Tongue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of then-current practice: mixing languages in performance makes dialogue unintelligible and absurd. Good practice: ensure intelligibility and coherence in dramatic/musical productions rather than fashionable foreign affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware translating sense to match musical meter (preserve semantic-melodic alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that translators altered sense to match English verse to Italian tunes (e.g., 'And turned my Rage, into Pity' → 'And into Pity turn'd my Rage'), producing mismatches where musical emphasis fell on semantically insignificant words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators/adapter should avoid sacrificing sense for metrical fit; ensure that musical stresses align with meaningful words/phrases. Anti-patterns: crafting English text only to fit tune numbers so that 'And' or other particles receive the melodic emphasis intended for emotionally significant words in the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural standard: prefer native arts and avoid uncritical foreign fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'At present, our Notions of Musick are so very uncertain, that we do not know what it is we like, only, in general, we are transported with any thing that is not English... our English Musick is quite rooted out, and nothing yet planted in its stead.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A normative stance: do not uncritically prefer foreign fashions (Italian music, etc.) at the expense of domestic arts; value balance so that music does not entirely displace other arts that refine human nature. Example/anti-pattern: giving Italian opera precedence over native tragedy like Phædra.
